Interviewer | How does this reach you as a councillor?

Speaker | Content
Interviewer | What did you do with it?
Respondent | Raised it in committee twice. The first time I got a written answer about detection accuracy, which wasn't the question I'd asked. The second time I asked for the raw logs and that's what eventually got the university their data. So it moved, but it moved because I had a committee to stand up in. A resident with the same observation has nowhere to go.

codes.rationale: Illustrates an initial lack of responsiveness, requiring repeated effort to obtain relevant data.

summary: The Ward Councillor's account highlights the crucial role of resident feedback in identifying issues with the adaptive traffic signal system, demonstrating a valuable source of data often overlooked by formal reports. A key theme is a lack of responsiveness from the council, evidenced by initial dismissive responses and the need for persistent advocacy to obtain relevant data. The councillor exhibits a strong degree of reflexivity, openly acknowledging their limited technical understanding and advocating for independent oversight to ensure accountability and responsiveness. Engagement is evident through the reliance on constituent observations, but the system's lack of responsiveness creates a barrier for residents to voice concerns. The councillor's call for an independent body suggests a recognition of the need for greater scrutiny and a more adaptive approach to governance.

Interview transcript G03 — Ward councillor, city council
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
Speaker | Content
Interviewer | How does this reach you as a councillor?
Respondent | Through my surgery, every other Saturday, three hours, anybody can come. In the first year after switch-on I'd say a dozen people raised the junctions. Not organised, not a campaign — individual people describing something specific about a crossing they use. That's the most reliable data I get about anything and it doesn't appear in any report.
Interviewer | What did people describe?
Respondent | Two themes. One was crossing time, particularly for older residents on the Alder Street junction. The other, which I didn't expect, was uncertainty — people saying they didn't know if it had seen them, so they'd press the button again, or step forward to be noticed, which is exactly what you don't want people doing.
Interviewer | What did you do with it?
Respondent | Raised it in committee twice. The first time I got a written answer about detection accuracy, which wasn't the question I'd asked. The second time I asked for the raw logs and that's what eventually got the university their data. So it moved, but it moved because I had a committee to stand up in. A resident with the same observation has nowhere to go.
Interviewer | Do you feel you understand the system well enough to scrutinise it?
Respondent | No. I'm a councillor, I do this alongside a job. I get a hundred-page pack the Friday before a Tuesday committee. I've read enough to ask about crossing times because a constituent taught me what to ask. I could not tell you how the model weighs a bus against a pedestrian and I've never been offered a briefing that would tell me.
Interviewer | What would help?
Respondent | Somebody independent who answers to the committee rather than to the department, with enough hours to actually read things. Every authority has internal audit for money. There's no equivalent for this, and this is now making decisions about people all day.
